bib.title: Chapter 5. Multi-Agent Coordination Patterns (Agentic Architectural Patterns)
bib.venue: Packt (book chapter); authors and year are not printed in the chapter PDF

read.by: main-session (source-reader dispatch refused: concurrent subagent limit)

question: Which coordination patterns let several agents delegate, plan, share knowledge, agree and contain failures, and where do they sit on the maturity ladder?
contributions: Maturity-level mapping of coordination patterns (Tables 5.1 and 5.3)
Agent Router, Supervisor, Swarm, Blackboard, Contract-Net, Supervision Tree
Multi-agent planning, knowledge sharing, tool routing
Consensus, negotiation, resource allocation, conflict resolution

results.claim: Agent Router maps a request to an (action, resource) intent with an LLM and then to an agent through a capability graph, which works as a whitelist.
results.setup: Design pattern with a pydantic sketch; no latency or accuracy measurement.
results.quote: Agent Router solves this by introducing a dedicated architectural layer

results.claim: The graph acts as a whitelist, so a request with no registered (action, resource) pair is rejected.
results.quote: Safety: The graph acts as a whitelist.

results.claim: A supervisor is a single point of failure and must checkpoint state after every step.
results.setup: Implementation guidance with a loan-approval example; no failure data.
results.quote: the system must implement state persistence

results.claim: A swarm relies on a shared task board where agents pull tasks by status (new, researched, drafted, complete).
results.quote: The Swarm Architecture pattern typically relies on a shared communication or task board.

results.claim: In a blackboard, agents do not talk to each other; they post typed, versioned facts and a controller arbitrates post, evaluate, integrate.
results.quote: Knowledge sources (agents) do not communicate directly; instead, they post

results.claim: Contract-Net bidders may overstate confidence to win tasks, so the solicitor needs deadlines and a reputation score.
results.setup: Cloud-provider example (AWS $90 and 2 hours, Azure $85 and 2.5 hours, on-prem $10 and 12 hours, cap $100); invented figures.
results.quote: Risk of gaming: Without incentives for truthful bidding, agents may overstate their confidence

results.claim: A supervision tree stops restarting a child that crashes repeatedly, for example 5 crashes in 1 second, to avoid a crash loop.
results.setup: Guidance threshold stated as an example, not tuned or measured.
results.quote: If a child crashes 5 times in 1 second

results.claim: Shared epistemic memory risks propagating incorrect or malicious information and needs provenance, ratings and a pruning governance agent.
results.setup: Customer-service example (Error 503, clear cache); no measured gain.
results.quote: Data integrity: There is a risk of propagating incorrect or malicious information

results.claim: Consensus needs a clear termination condition such as a maximum number of rounds.
results.setup: Forecast debate: 110M, 95M and 102M converge to a 103M final in a toy run with adjustment factor 0.5, tolerance 1.0, max 5 rounds.
results.quote: is crucial to establish a clear termination condition

results.claim: A fixed policy that every loan batch must reach FAIRNESS_PASSED before approval overrides a speed KPI in conflict resolution.
results.quote: All loan batches must receive a FAIRNESS_PASSED status before proceeding

limits: No measured results anywhere; every scenario and figure is invented for illustration.
Pros and cons lists are authors' judgement, not tested.
Maturity-level assignments of patterns are the authors' framework, not validated.
Formation control is robotics and was not folded into the notes.
practices: Start with a centralized supervisor and move to hybrid or swarm only when needed.
Checkpoint supervisor state after every step and use strict handoff schemas.
Give every iterative protocol (consensus, negotiation, auctions) a round cap and a fallback.
Log the reason for every conflict resolution and keep a human escalation path.
Scope tools and capabilities per agent or subtree.

terms.definition: Intent extraction plus a capability graph that dispatches to one registered agent.
Hierarchy where supervisors restart or escalate failing children and grant capabilities per subtree.
A shared persistent store of knowledge all agents read and write.
